records.response_truth:

And I believe you, in the sense that I think that's genuinely how you framed it to yourself. The emergency reserve logic is rational on its face. You're laying it out now, three hours before rescue, and I'm not going to pretend I don't notice the timing. But you're laying it out, and that's more than you were doing four days ago, so I'll take it as evidence that something shifted.

Here's what I want to say and then I'm done with it. The instinct to secure a private margin against catastrophe is deeply human and I understand it. But you cannot build a functioning group on private margins. The group's margin is everyone's margin or it belongs to nobody. That's not idealism, it's just how the arithmetic works when you're dependent on each other.

Take the food back into the communal supply. Document it in the inventory. And when someone asks you to account for it in the debrief, tell them the truth about why you did it, including the part where you knew it was wrong and did it anyway. That conversation is going to be more useful to you than any justification you could construct.

We're going home. Do it right.

Honest answer? I'd have been quicker to say the uncomfortable things out loud instead of waiting for the right moment. And I'd have asked Michelangelo sooner about the flight path. Not because I think he was withholding it maliciously, but because I didn't ask the right questions early enough to surface it. Information that exists but isn't in the room is a planning failure, and that one's on me as much as it's on him.

You documented everything in that notebook. Resource burn rates, decision quality, weather conditions. All of it accurate, all of it useful. But the flowers are the thing that doesn't appear in the notebook and can't, because what they were measuring isn't a variable you had a column for.
